items.title: CMV: A car approaching a 4-way stop should be able to treat it as a yield so long as there is clearly nobody else approaching.
items.text:
CMV: A car approaching a 4-way stop should be able to treat it as a yield so long as there is clearly nobody else approaching.
[removed]
I cannot find a single piece of evidence online to support this
How is this any different than if it occured at a regular cross walk? The cross walk is what gives the pedestrian the right of way. Not the stop sign.
A police officer can pull you over and ticket you for not coming to a complete stop. That is the law as it is written.
Are bikes allowed to just randomly cut into the street with no regard for oncoming traffic?
A parked police car or a police car driving behind me.
What if the police officer is driving behind me?

I can’t find anything that supports this. Crosswalks give pedestrians the right of way. They are regularly found at 4 way stops, but it is not the 4 way stop itself establishing the pedestrian’s right of way.
You just quoted something that I literally never said.

I think you’re trying to play semantics. A parked police officer is certainly not actively approaching anything, so no, at least one of those two scenarios do not qualify as approaching.

In regards to the police officer behind you, sure, they are approaching. But there is no scenario where they could ever have the right of way over you, so their existence is irrelevant outside of their ticketing ability.
So then you believe all yield signs should be converted to stop signs due to this reasoning, correct?
If visibility is low, you cannot make your decision to yield until you have accessed proper lines of sight.
What if the police officer is behind you? Nobody relevant to the 4 way stop is approaching, yet you could still get ticketed.

Yes, but the police officer approaching the intersection from behind has zero ambiguity in regards to who has the right of the way at the upcoming intersection. They are no more relevant than a car passing you in the opposite direction.
This seems like you are trying to argue semantics, unless you can provide even a single way in which a car behind you plays a role in your interaction with the 4 way stop.

What if a car stops in the middle of the road in front of you for no reason?  The back car is expected to keep enough distance to avoid collision.

And this is not semantics. Maybe I should rephrase it to: if you have a clear path to the intersection, and the other 3 roads clearly have nobody approaching the intersection, you should be legally allowed to treat it as a yield.
